claim: Mice have a large visual field that is constantly stabilized by vestibular ocular reflex (VOR) driven eye rotations that counter head-rotations.
source: Mice have a large visual field that is constantly stabilized by vestibular ocular reflex (VOR) driven eye rotations that counter head-rotations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work (Meyer et al., 2020; Meyer et al., 2018; Michaiel et al., 2020; Payne and Raymond, 2017; Wallace et al., 2013) throughout the manuscript.

claim: During pursuit, the prey image consistently falls within a small area of the VOR-stabilized visual field.
source: we show that the prey image consistently falls within a small area of the VOR-stabilized visual field.
evidence: Supported by probability density maps in Figure 2G and H showing cricket positions clustered in a localized region during tracking epochs.

claim: The functional focus coincides with the region of minimal optic flow within the visual field.
source: This functional focus coincides with the region of minimal optic flow within the visual field and consequently area of minimal motion-induced image-blur, as during pursuit mice ran directly toward the prey.
evidence: Demonstrated by optic flow analysis in Figure 6E showing overlap between optic flow minima and functional foci.

claim: The functional focus lies in the upper-temporal part of the retina.
source: The functional focus lies in the upper-temporal part of the retina and coincides with the reported high density-region of Alpha-ON sustained retinal ganglion cells.
evidence: Shown through eye model projections in Figure 3 comparing functional focus location to RGC density distributions.

claim: The functional focus coincides with the reported high density-region of Alpha-ON sustained retinal ganglion cells.
source: The functional focus lies in the upper-temporal part of the retina and coincides with the reported high density-region of Alpha-ON sustained retinal ganglion cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by overlap analysis in Figure 3E showing 35-67% overlap with highest density Alpha-ON sustained RGCs (Bleckert et al., 2014).

claim: Removing both olfactory and auditory cues approximately doubled the average time to capture a cricket compared to removal of auditory cues alone.
source: By removing both olfactory and auditory cues, the average time to capture a cricket approximately doubled compared to removal of auditory cues alone (time to capture, median ± SD, control 24.92 ± 16.77 s, olfactory and auditory cues removed, 43.51 ± 27.82 s, p = 0.0471, Wilcoxon rank sum test, N=13 control and 12 cue removed trials from N = 5 mice).
evidence: Statistical comparison provided with specific values and p-value from experimental data.

claim: Mice have monocular visual fields of around 200 degrees.
source: predator detection in mice is served by a panoramic visual field which is achieved by the lateral placement of the eyes in the head (Dräger, 1978; Hughes, 1979; Oommen and Stahl, 2008) combined with monocular visual fields of around 200 degrees (Dräger and Olsen, 1980; Hughes, 1979; Sterratt et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from multiple published sources on mouse visual field anatomy.

claim: Eye movements in freely moving mice constantly stabilize the animal's visual field by counteracting head rotations through the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR).
source: In addition, eye movements in freely moving mice constantly stabilize the animal's visual field by counteracting head rotations through the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) (Meyer et al., 2020; Meyer et al., 2018; Michaiel et al., 2020; Payne and Raymond, 2017) maintaining the large panoramic overhead view (Wallace et al., 2013) critical for predator detection (Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent studies on mouse VOR.

claim: Mouse retina contains retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) with a broad diversity of functional classes.
source: Mouse retina contains retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), the output cells of the retina, with a broad diversity of functional classes (Baden et al., 2016; Bleckert et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from multiple studies characterizing RGC diversity.

claim: The highest overall density of RGCs faces laterally given the lateral eye position.
source: Given the lateral eye position, the highest overall density faces laterally (Dräger and Olsen, 1981; Sabbah et al., 2017; Salinas-Navarro et al., 2009; Stabio et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from multiple anatomical studies of mouse retina.

claim: Functionally defined ganglion cells and cone sub-types are segregated into retinal subregions within the large stabilized field of view.
source: Further, as the functionally defined ganglion cells (Baden et al., 2016; Bleckert et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2012) and cone sub-types (Szél et al., 1992) are segregated into retinal subregions within the large stabilized field of view, recent studies suggest that retinal subregions are tuned for specific behavioral tasks depending on what part of the world they subtend (Baden et al., 2016; Bleckert et al., 2014; Hughes, 1977; Sabbah et al., 2017; Szatko et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from multiple studies on retinal organization and function.

claim: Upon cricket detection, mice oriented and ran towards the cricket, resulting in a significant adjustment to their trajectory.
source: Upon cricket detection, mice oriented and ran towards the cricket, resulting in a significant adjustment to their trajectory (Δ target bearing: 40.2 ± 35.1°, P = 6.20 x 10−10, Δ speed: 10.2 ± 7.4 cm/s, P = 1.91 x 10−10; N=57 detect-track sequences N = 3 mice; Paired Wilcoxon's signed rank test for both tests)
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with specific values and significance tests.

claim: During tracking, the cricket was kept in front of the mouse, resulting in a significant reduction in the spread of target bearings compared to during detect epochs.
source: During tracking, the cricket was kept in front of the mouse, resulting in a significant reduction in the spread of target bearings compared to during detect epochs (Figure 2D, Target bearing: detect 6.2 ± 62.1°, track: 2.5 ± 25.6°, mean ± SD, Brown-Forsythe test p = 0, F statistic=7.05x103, N=4406 detect and 13624 track frames, N=3 mice), consistent with previous findings (Hoy et al., 2016).
evidence: Statistical comparison of behavioral data with reference to previous study.

claim: The location of the cricket image during the tracking phase was significantly different from the cluster in the detect epoch.
source: average histogram of the location of cricket image during tracking phase vs average histogram of the location of cricket during detect phase: Left eye P = 3.54 x 10−46, Right eye P = 1.08 x 10−81, differences calculated by taking the Mean Absolute Difference with bootstrapping, N=57 detect-track sequences, N = 3 mice
evidence: Statistical comparison of cricket position distributions between behavioral epochs.

claim: The functional focus fell within the binocular field.
source: Thus, during the tracking and pursuit behavior the image of the prey consistently fell on a local and specific retinal area that we refer to from here on as the functional focus. The functional focus fell within the binocular field
evidence: Shown in Figure 2G-H with functional focus located in binocular region.

claim: The region of elevated density of RGCs has been found to be located near the optical axis.
source: while the region of elevated density of RGCs has been found to be located near the optical axis (Dräger and Olsen, 1981)
evidence: Cited from anatomical study of mouse retina.

claim: The location of the retinal specialization may not overlap with the functional focus.
source: which suggests that the location of the retinal specialization may not overlap with the functional focus.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of RGC density location and functional focus location.

claim: The gain of compensation for head pitch and roll rotations was relatively linear and less than unity, indicating on average under-compensation of the head rotation.
source: The gain of this compensation was relatively linear and less than unity for both pitch- and roll-axes, indicating on average under-compensation of the head rotation (slope (gain) of relation for pitch axis, −0.45 ± 0.12 and −0.48 ± 0.06; roll axis −0.51 ± 0.12 and −0.62 ± 0.05 for left and right eye respectively, 168852 frames, N=3 mice).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of head-eye rotation relationships from experimental data.

claim: For rotations around the head x-axis (head pitch changes) the gain of compensation was most affected by freezing torsional rotations.
source: For rotations around the head x-axis (head pitch changes) the gain of compensation was most affected by freezing torsional rotations (Figure 4C, gain mean ± SD, control: −0.45 ± 0.12and-0.48 ± 0.06; torsion frozen −0.24 ± 0.1 and −0.24 ± 0.01, for left and right eyes respectively, N = 168852 frames, N=3 mice)
evidence: Computational analysis freezing specific eye rotation axes to assess their contribution.

claim: The gain of compensation for rotations around the head y-axis (head roll changes) was dramatically affected by freezing vertical rotations.
source: The gain of compensation for rotations around the head y-axis (head roll changes) was dramatically affected by freezing vertical rotations (Figure 4C, gain mean ± SD, control: −0.51 ± 0.12 and −0.62 ± 0.05, vertical frozen −0.16 ± 0.14 and −0.17 ± 0.03, for left and right eyes respectively, N = 168852 frames, N=3 mice)
evidence: Computational analysis freezing specific eye rotation axes to assess their contribution.

claim: The functional foci for both eyes were predominately contained within the region of continuous binocular overlap.
source: The functional foci for both eyes were predominately contained within the region of continuous binocular overlap.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4D with functional foci overlaid on binocular overlap probability map.

claim: The mean alignment of the reference point over all animals and data segments was approximately 8-9 degrees.
source: the mean alignment of the reference point over all animals and data segments being ~8–9°, which is around the size of V1 cortical neuron receptive fields (~5–15° [Niell and Stryker, 2008], Figure 4H, mean ± SD, left eye projected into right eye 8.8 ± 6.9°; right eye projected into left eye 8.6 ± 6.7°).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of inter-ocular alignment with comparison to V1 receptive field sizes.

claim: Freezing the movements of one eye to its mean position resulted in a significant increase in the alignment error.
source: Coordination of eye movements was important for alignment, as freezing the movements of one eye to its mean position resulted in a significant increase in the alignment error when comparing individual cricket tracking sequences (left all rotations vs. left eye frozen P = 1.78 x 10−10, right eye all rotations vs. right eye frozen P = 7.12 x 10−11, N=52 sequences, unpaired Student's t-test)
evidence: Statistical comparison of alignment with and without eye movements frozen.

claim: As the mouse approached the cricket during the track behavioral epoch, the projected cricket positions systematically shifted lower in the visual field.
source: As the mouse approached the cricket during the track behavioral epoch, the projected cricket positions systematically shifted lower in the visual field (Figure 5A lower).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A with cricket positions color-coded by distance.

claim: Mice did not use additional head or eye movements to bring the cricket into the functional foci.
source: This suggests that the mice did not use additional head or eye movements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) to bring the cricket into the functional foci, but rather manipulated the cricket's position in the eye view by orienting and moving towards the target.
evidence: Inferred from systematic shift in cricket position and lack of compensatory head/eye movements.

claim: Head pitch remained stable as the mice approached the crickets.
source: Consistent with this, head pitch remained stable as the mice approached the crickets (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5B plotting head pitch vs distance to cricket.

claim: There was no significant difference in head pitch as a function of distance to the cricket between non-tracking and tracking periods.
source: Furthermore, there was no significant difference in head pitch as a function of distance to the cricket between non-tracking and tracking periods (non-tracking head pitch: −3.7 ± 26.5°, mean ± SD, median = −11.3°, tracking head pitch: −12.9 ± 15.7°, mean ± SD, median = −14.6°, Ks test, P = 0.709, paired Student's t-test P = 0.197, N = 18 non-tracking and track sequences, N = 3 mice).
evidence: Statistical comparison of head pitch between behavioral epochs.

claim: Mice did not significantly converge their eyes as they approached the crickets.
source: In addition, and consistent with previous findings (Michaiel et al., 2020), mice did not significantly converge their eyes as they approached the crickets (non-tracking head vergence: 7.6 ± 13.5°, mean ± SD, median = 8.6°, tracking head vergence: 2.5 ± 16.7°, mean ± SD, median = 3.2°. Ks test, P = 0.425, paired Student's t-test P = 0.225, N=18 non-tracking and track sequences, N = 3 mice, Figure 5—figure supplement 1J and Table 4).
evidence: Statistical analysis of vergence with citation to previous study.

claim: During cricket tracking periods, mice ran directly toward the cricket, and their trajectories were significantly straighter than during equivalent non-tracking phases.
source: During cricket tracking periods, mice ran directly toward the cricket, and their trajectories were significantly straighter than during equivalent non-tracking phases (Figure 5C–G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C-G with multiple trajectory metrics compared between epochs.

claim: Lateral deviation at the half-way point was significantly smaller in the tracking epochs compared to non-tracking epochs.
source: Lateral deviation at the half-way point (Figure 5E, non-tracking 4.3 ± 4.0 cm, tracking 1.4 ± 2.0 cm, p = 0.009)
evidence: Statistical comparison of trajectory metrics between behavioral epochs.

claim: Maximum lateral deviation was significantly smaller in tracking epochs compared to non-tracking epochs.
source: maximum lateral deviation (Figure 5F, non-tracking, 7.7 ± 4.9 cm, tracking 2.8 ± 2.0 cm, p = 0.0006)
evidence: Statistical comparison of trajectory metrics between behavioral epochs.

claim: The area between the trajectory and minimum distance path to the target was significantly smaller in tracking epochs compared to non-tracking epochs.
source: the area between the trajectory and minimum distance path to the target (Figure 5G, area under the curve, non-tracking 135.6 ± 102.7 cm2, tracking 51.3 ± 45.8 cm2, p = 0.0029)
evidence: Statistical comparison of trajectory metrics between behavioral epochs.

claim: Mice do not make compensatory vertical head movements, tracking eye movements or vergence eye movements to keep prey within their functional foci.
source: Together this suggests that mice do not make compensatory vertical head movements, tracking eye movements or vergence eye movements to keep prey within their functional foci, but instead retain their target within a restricted bearing by running straight towards it.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of head and eye movements during pursuit.

claim: Optic flow is minimized in the direction of travel directly in front of the animal.
source: Optic flow is minimized in the direction of travel directly in front of the animal (Sabbah et al., 2017), with flow fields directed away from the travel direction and forming a second minimum directly behind the animal's head (Figure 6A, see also Angelaki and Hess, 2005).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on optic flow.

claim: Mice have laterally facing eyes with optical axis approximately 60 degrees lateral of frontal.
source: As mice have laterally facing eyes (optical axis = 59.9 ± 19.8° and −62.3 ± 14.7° lateral of frontal for the left and right eyes respectively, N=3 mice)
evidence: Measured from anatomical calibration data.

claim: Idealized forward motion resulted in the region of minimal optic flow in each eye being located off optical axis in the ventro-medial corneal region representing the animal's forward direction.
source: idealized forward motion resulted in the region of minimal optic flow in each eye being located off optical axis in the ventro-medial corneal region representing the animal's forward direction (radial displacement from optical axis 36.64 ± 0.92° and −41.11 ± 2.27°, rotational angle 122.95 ± 17.05° and −107.94 ± 9.96°, for the left and right eyes respectively, mean ± SD, N=2 mice, Figure 6C).
evidence: Calculated from idealized optic flow simulation.

claim: Optic flow in the 30x30° region surrounding the ventro-medial point of minimal optic flow was significantly lower than that in an equivalent region in the ventro-temporal region during free movement.
source: Optic flow in the 30x30° region surrounding the ventro-medial point of minimal optic flow was significantly lower than that in an equivalent region in the ventro-temporal region during free movement, but not in the simulated case (free movement: nasal 46.3 ± 9.8 °/s, temporal: 199.4 ± 29.0 °/s, p = 0.0014, simulated: nasal 163.6 ± 82.2 °/s, temporal: 833.0 ± 416.5 °/s, p = 0.0662, mean ± SD, two-sided t-test, unequal variance, N=2 mice).
evidence: Statistical comparison of optic flow in different regions.

claim: Optic flow was higher in the lower visual field and considerably lower in the upper visual field.
source: Optic flow was higher in the lower visual field and considerably lower in the upper visual field (lower left eye visual field: 262.44 ± 106.50 °/s, upper left eye visual field: 44.87 ± 24.31 °/s, p = 1.78x10−20, lower right eye visual field: 361.91 ± 168.80 °/s, upper right eye visual field: 40.59 ± 22.79 °/s, p = 6.68x10−19, Two-sided t-test, unequal variance, N=2 mice)
evidence: Statistical comparison of optic flow in upper vs lower visual fields.

claim: The region of highest likelihood for the presence of the optic flow minimum overlapped considerably with the functional foci in both eyes during the tracking epochs of the pursuit behavior.
source: The region of highest likelihood for the presence of the optic flow minimum overlapped considerably with the functional foci in both eyes during the tracking epochs of the pursuit behavior (overlap of optic flow 95% minima and functional foci 50% regions: 100% and 99 ± 1%, overlap of optic flow 50% minima and functional foci 50% regions: 61 ± 14% and 72 ± 4% in left and right eyes respectively, N=3 mice, Figure 6E).
evidence: Quantitative overlap analysis between optic flow minima and functional foci.

claim: The behavioral strategy employed by mice during hunting results in the image of their prey coinciding with the region of reduced optic flow during pursuit.
source: Together this shows that the behavioral strategy employed by mice during hunting, consisting of orienting themselves to directly face the prey and following a straight and direct course to it, results in the image of their prey coinciding with the region of reduced optic flow during pursuit, where the retinal image of their prey is least distorted due to motion induced image blur.
evidence: Synthesized conclusion from optic flow and behavioral trajectory analyses.

claim: Eye rotations in mice primarily stabilize their large field of view and all three rotational axes, including ocular torsion, combine to counter head rotations.
source: This strongly suggested that eye-rotations in mice, like in rats, primarily stabilize their large field of view and that all three rotational axes, including ocular torsion, combine to counter head rotations.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of head-eye rotation relationships across all three axes.

claim: Eye rotations cannot be predicted from head rotations in any one axis but rather by a combination of all head rotations.
source: In addition, we also show that eye rotations cannot be predicted from head rotations in any one axis as has been suggested by recent studies of mouse eye motion (Meyer et al., 2020; Meyer et al., 2018; Michaiel et al., 2020) but rather by a combination of all head rotations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 with model predictions using single vs multiple head rotation axes.

claim: The location of the functional focus occurs within a dorso-temporal retinal region in an area with the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs.
source: Using this we show that the location of the functional focus occurs within a dorso-temporal retinal region in an area with the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs, whose general properties have been previously proposed to be well suited for this purpose (Bleckert et al., 2014).
evidence: Shown through eye model projection and overlap analysis with RGC density maps.

claim: The binocular region of the visual field in mice is contained within the nasal visual field of each eye, and spans a region of 30-40° in front of the animal.
source: Both estimates of the field of view of the mouse eye (Dräger, 1978) and electrophysiological measurements of receptive field locations of visually responsive neurons (Dräger and Olsen, 1980; Wagor et al., 1980) have established that the binocular region of the visual field in mice is contained within the nasal visual field of each eye, and spans a region of 30-40° in front of the animal (Wagor et al., 1980).
evidence: Cited from previous anatomical and electrophysiological studies.

claim: The overlapping monocular fields that make up the binocular overlap are not constantly maintained but fluctuate at the margins as the eyes rotate to counter head rotations.
source: We present here, that similar to the rat (Wallace et al., 2013), the overlapping monocular fields that make up the binocular overlap are not constantly maintained (Figure 4H) but fluctuate at the margins as the eyes rotate to counter head rotations (Figure 4D), resulting in a region where there is a transition from one area with near continuous binocular coverage, through to a region that is invariably monocular.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4D and 4H with binocular overlap probability maps.

claim: The functional focus lies within the region of high probability of maintained binocular overlap.
source: The functional focus described here lies within the region of high probability of maintained binocular overlap.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4D with functional focus overlaid on binocular overlap map.

claim: The temporal retina contains both ipsilaterally projecting (uncrossed) RGCs and RGCs which form part of the callosal projection pathway.
source: This region of the visual field projects onto the temporal retina, which contains both ipsilaterally projecting (uncrossed) RGCs (Dräger and Olsen, 1980; Reese and Cowey, 1986) and RGCs which form part of the callosal projection pathway (Laing et al., 2015; Olavarria and Van Sluyters, 1983; Ramachandra et al., 2020), both of which are considered central to binocular visual processing.
evidence: Cited from multiple studies on retinal projections.

claim: The functional focus location is well placed to support stereoscopic depth perception.
source: In addition, the current study adds to the significance of these previous findings and suggests that the functional focus location is well placed to support stereoscopic depth perception, assuming that this form of visual processing is available to and employed by the mouse (La Chioma et al., 2019; La Chioma et al., 2020; Samonds et al., 2019; Scholl et al., 2013; Scholl et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from functional focus location in binocular region with citations to studies on mouse stereopsis.

claim: Selective ablation of ipsilaterally projecting RGCs in the ventro-temporal retina reduced the probability that coming into close proximity with the cricket resulted in its capture.
source: Further supportive of the importance and relevance of the region of binocular overlap, another recent study provides strong evidence to suggest that ipsilaterally projecting RGCs in the ventro-temporal retina are important in the final phase of cricket pursuit (mouse to cricket distance less than 6 cm), with selective ablation of these RGCs reducing the probability that coming into close proximity with the cricket resulted in its capture (Johnson et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from recent study on RGC function in prey capture.

claim: The overall highest density of retinal ganglion cells in mice is located in the region around the optical axis.
source: While the overall highest density of retinal ganglion cells in mice is located in the region around the optical axis (Dräger and Olsen, 1981)
evidence: Cited from anatomical study of mouse retina.

claim: The highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs resides in the superior-temporal retina.
source: a recent study examining the distributions of various different subclasses of RGCs has shown that the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs resides in the superior-temporal retina (Bleckert et al., 2014)
evidence: Cited from study on RGC subtype distributions.

claim: Alpha-ON sustained RGCs have center-surround receptive fields, a rapid response and fast conducting axon, and are thought to be 'spot detectors'.
source: These Alpha-ON sustained RGCs have center-surround receptive fields, a rapid response and fast conducting axon, and are thought to be 'spot detectors' (for review see Dhande et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from review on RGC properties.

claim: Alpha-ON sustained RGCs in the superior-temporal retinal region have a significantly smaller dendritic tree radius and subtend a smaller area of physical space as well as have overlapping receptive fields compared to the same RGC-type in other regions of the retina.
source: In addition, the Alpha-ON sustained RGCs in this particular retinal region differ from the same RGC-type in other regions of the retina as they have a significantly smaller dendritic tree radius and subtend a smaller area of physical space as well as have overlapping receptive fields (Bleckert et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from study on regional RGC properties.

claim: The cellular properties of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs as well as the region in-front of the animal which provides their input are consistent with the requirements for tracking small and mobile targets.
source: Taken together, the cellular properties as well as the region in-front of the animal which provides their input are consistent with the requirements for tracking small and mobile targets (Bleckert et al., 2014; Dean et al., 1989; Lettvin et al., 1959; Procacci et al., 2020).
evidence: Synthesized from RGC properties with citations to studies on target tracking.

claim: Both wide-field and narrow-field neuronal types in the mouse superior colliculus play central roles in the detection and pursuit phases of prey pursuit, respectively.
source: A recent study has shown that both wide-field and narrow-field neuronal types in the mouse superior colliculus play central roles in the detection and pursuit phases of this pursuit task, respectively (Hoy et al., 2019)
evidence: Cited from study on superior colliculus function in prey pursuit.

claim: Alpha-ON sustained RGCs have projections to the superior colliculus.
source: and consistent with this, Alpha-ON sustained RGCs having projections to the superior colliculus (Martersteck et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from study on RGC projection patterns.

claim: Alpha RGCs have strong projections to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus and thus V1.
source: It is currently unclear how the primary visual cortex (V1) contributes to this behavior, but some role is possible if not probable, which would also be supported by the strong Alpha RGC projection to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus and thus V1 (Martersteck et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from study on RGC projection patterns with speculation about V1 role.

claim: An increased cortical magnification factor occurs in the region corresponding to the nasal, binocular visual field.
source: Additionally, an increased cortical magnification factor occurs in the region corresponding to the nasal, binocular visual field (Garrett et al., 2014; Schuett et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from studies on cortical visual field representation.

claim: Global alignment across the retina of the preferred orientation of direction-selective retinal ganglion cells with the cardinal directions of optic flow during idealized motion has been shown in mice.
source: Mechanistically supporting this, global alignment across the retina of the preferred orientation of direction-selective retinal ganglion cells with the cardinal directions of optic flow during idealized motion has been shown in mice (Sabbah et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from study on direction-selective RGC organization.

claim: Ocular torsion in freely moving rats is correlated with head pitch such that nose-up rotation of the head is counteracted by incyclotorsion of both eyes, with nose-down pitch counteracted by excyclotorsion.
source: In freely moving rats, it has been shown that ocular torsion is correlated with head pitch such that nose-up rotation of the head is counteracted by incyclotorsion (rotation toward the nose) of both eyes, with nose-down pitch counteracted by excyclotorsion (Wallace et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous study on rat VOR.

claim: Torsional rotation in freely moving mice is dynamic, with episodes showing in- and excyclovergence as well as dextro- and levocycloversion.
source: We show here that torsional rotation in freely moving mice is also dynamic, with episodes showing in- and excyclovergence as well as dextro- and levocycloversion.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 with examples of different torsional coordination patterns.

claim: There was an additional relation between ocular torsion and head roll consistent with VOR-evoked dextro- and levocycloversion.
source: Further, while the correlation between torsional rotation and head pitch observed in rats was measured, there was also an additional relation between ocular torsion and head roll consistent with VOR-evoked dextro- and levocycloversion.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2L-M with correlation between torsion and head roll.

claim: Prediction of torsion using a model based on head pitch alone resulted in an average error of around 7°.
source: Consequently, prediction of torsion using a model based on head pitch alone resulted in an average error of around 7°, while an expanded model including roll as well performed better (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–O).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2J-O comparing model predictions.

claim: During pursuit in mice the image of the intended prey falls consistently in a localized region of their visual fields through the animal orientating their head and body and running directly toward the prey rather than with specific eye movements.
source: In summary, we show here that during pursuit in mice the image of the intended prey falls consistently in a localized region of their visual fields, referred to here as the functional focus, and that this occurs through the animal orientating their head and body and running directly toward the prey rather than with specific eye movements.
evidence: Summary conclusion synthesized from behavioral and eye movement analyses.

claim: The location of the functional focus is within the binocular visual field and coincides with the region of minimal optic flow during the pursuit.
source: The location of the functional focus is within the binocular visual field, but in addition also coincides with the region of minimal optic flow during the pursuit, and presumably also minimally distorted by motion blur.
evidence: Summary conclusion from binocular overlap and optic flow analyses.

claim: Experiments were carried out using male C57Bl/6J mice acquired from Charles River Laboratories.
source: Experiments were carried out using male C57Bl/6J mice acquired from Charles River Laboratories.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods.

claim: At the time of the cricket hunting experiments, mice were between 2 and 8 months old, and weighed between 21 and 29 g.
source: At the time of the cricket hunting experiments, mice (n=9) were between 2 and 8 months old, and weighed between 21 and 29 g.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods.

claim: During experiments in which head and eye rotations were recorded cricket body sizes ranged from 1 cm to 2 cm.
source: During experiments in which head and eye rotations were recorded cricket body sizes ranged from 1 cm to 2 cm (1.8 ± 0.3 cm, mean ± SD, n=25).
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods.

claim: The average differences in position of fiducial points between the two coordinate systems were less than 1 mm.
source: The average differences in position of fiducial points between the two coordinate systems were less than 1 mm (mean ± SD, x position, 0.18 ± 3.1 mm, y position, 0.07 ± 1.6 mm, z position, 0.66 ± 1.8 mm, N=54 fiducial points from three datasets).
evidence: Stated in Results describing coordinate system registration accuracy.

claim: The average 50% contour of the functional focus was overlapped by the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGC's by 35% and 67% for left and right eye respectively.
source: The average 50% contour of the functional focus was overlapped by the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGC's by 35% and 67% for left and right eye respectively (Figure 3E, black, mean ± SD for left and right eye, 35.1 ± 19.8%, 66.7 ± 0.09%, p = 0.095 and 0.019, one-sided Student's t-test)
evidence: Quantitative overlap analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The overlap of the functional focus with the second highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs was 83% and 95% for left and right eye respectively.
source: and the overlap with the second highest density was 83% and 95% (mean ± SD for left and right eye, 82.8 ± 20.1%, 94.8 ± 24.7%, p = 0.042 and 0.003, one-sided Student's t-test)
evidence: Quantitative overlap analysis with statistical testing.

claim: There is a high degree of correspondence between the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGC's and the functional focus during pursuit behavior.
source: suggesting a high degree of correspondence between the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGC's and the functional focus during pursuit behavior.
evidence: Inferred from overlap analysis results.

claim: Objects falling within the functional foci are processed by Alpha-ON sustained RGC's.
source: Together this suggests that objects falling within the functional foci are processed by Alpha-ON sustained RGC's.
evidence: Inferred from spatial correspondence between functional foci and Alpha-ON sustained RGC density.

claim: Torsional rotations in freely moving mice spanned a wide range of rotation angles.
source: As with the vertical and horizontal rotations (Meyer et al., 2018), torsional rotations in freely moving mice spanned a wide range of rotation angles (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D)
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D with distribution of torsional angles.

claim: Torsional rotations were correlated with head pitch with Pearson's correlation coefficient of -0.72 and 0.58 for detect, and -0.60 and 0.53 for track in left and right eyes respectively.
source: and were correlated with head pitch (Pearson's correlation coefficient (r): detect −0.72, 0.58, track: −0.60 and 0.53 for left and right eyes respectively, N=4406 detect and 13624 track frames, N=3 mice, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–D)
evidence: Correlation analysis of torsion and head pitch.

claim: Torsional rotations were correlated with head roll with Pearson's correlation coefficient of -0.46 and -0.47 for detect, and -0.45 and -0.48 for track in left and right eyes respectively.
source: as well as head roll (Pearson's correlation coefficient (r): detect: −0.46, –0.47 track: −0.45 and −0.48 for left and right eyes respectively, N=4406 detect and 13624 track frames, N=3 mice, Figure 4—figure supplement 2L–M)
evidence: Correlation analysis of torsion and head roll.

claim: The functional foci were directed at the region in front of the animal's nose and within the region of stable binocular overlap.
source: Viewed from above the animal's head, the functional foci were directed at the region in front of the animal's nose and within the region of stable binocular overlap (azimuth: 1.4 ± 8.8° and −4.4 ± 9.3°, elevation 5.7 ± 2.1° and 4.9 ± 1.4° for left and right eyes respectively, N = 13641 frames, N=3 mice)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of functional focus direction in head-centered coordinates.

claim: The retinal specialization was directed laterally.
source: while the retinal specialization was directed laterally (azimuth: −66.2 ± 6.7° and 70.3 ± 4.7°, elevation: 30.8 ± 12.2° and 41.0 ± 13.5° for left and right eyes respectively, N = 13641 frames N=3 mice. Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of RGC density peak direction in head-centered coordinates.

claim: The Alpha-ON sustained RGC's were directed in front of the animal's nose.
source: The Alpha-ON sustained RGC's were also directed in front of the animal's nose (mean ± SD, elevation:16.0 ± 6.9° and 10.8 ± 11.0°, azimuth: −3.6 ± 0.7° and 5.8 ± 7.9° for left and right eyes respectively, N = 168400 frames, N = 3 mice, Figure 3F).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of Alpha-ON sustained RGC density direction in head-centered coordinates.

claim: The relatively linear relationships between head and eye rotation around the head pitch and roll axes with a transition through the origin suggests that the horizontal, vertical and torsional eye movements are combined to effectively compensate pitch- and roll-related head movements.
source: The relatively linear relationships between head and eye rotation around the head pitch and roll axes (Figure 4B) with a transition through the origin suggests that the horizontal, vertical and torsional eye movements are combined to effectively compensate pitch- and roll-related head movements.
evidence: Inferred from linear head-eye rotation relationships shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Freezing torsion also reduced compensation gain for head roll but to a lesser extent than freezing vertical rotations.
source: with freezing torsion also reducing compensation gain but to a lesser extent (Figure 4C, Table 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C and Table 3 comparing effects of freezing different eye rotation axes.

claim: The average alignment error in the functional foci was 8-10 degrees.
source: and that the average alignment error in the functional foci was 8–10°.
evidence: Calculated from inter-ocular alignment analysis in functional focus region.

claim: Freezing eye movements resulted in approximately 54% increase in the mean alignment error over all frames for the reference location.
source: and a ~54% increase in the mean alignment error over all frames for the reference location (Figure 4I, left eye projected into right eye (left eye frozen) 13.4 ± 8.3°; Right eye projected into left eye (right eye frozen) 13.4 ± 8.3°, mean ± SD, 159318 frames, N=3 mice)
evidence: Quantitative comparison of alignment error with and without eye movements.

claim: Crickets provided a prey target that could successfully evade capture for extended periods of time.
source: Crickets (Acheta domesticus), shown previously to be readily pursued and preyed upon by laboratory mice (Hoy et al., 2016), provided a prey target that could successfully evade capture for extended periods of time (total time for each cricket before capture: 64.4 ± 39.3 s, average time ± SD, N = 21 crickets and three mice, Video 4 and 5).
evidence: Measured from behavioral experiments with citation to previous study.

claim: The presence of the TiO2 marks did not significantly change the animal's cricket hunting performance as assessed by the average time taken to capture crickets.
source: The presence of the TiO2 marks did not significantly change the animal's cricket hunting performance as assessed by the average time taken to capture crickets (Figure 7C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7C comparing capture times with and without TiO2 spots.

claim: The maximum deviations in the eye model due to 10, 50, and 100 µm changes in optical parameters were 0.4, 1.38 and 2.76 degrees respectively.
source: The maximum deviations were 0.4, 1.38 and 2.76 degrees for the 10, 50, and 100 µm changes, respectively (Figure 7E), and overall, none of the observed effects on the model would influence the conclusions drawn from the analyses performed using the eye model.
evidence: Sensitivity analysis of eye model parameters shown in Figure 7E.
